name: Ulomoides dermestoides

card.summary: A small darkling beetle swallowed live as a folk remedy for inflammatory and respiratory complaints, with online interest in general health claims.
card.aka: Chinese beetle; peanut beetle; cancer beetle; asthma beetle; Chinese weevil
card.note: Defensive secretions are cytotoxic; overconsumption has been linked to serious complications.

quick.overview:
Ulomoides dermestoides is a grain-pest darkling beetle native to Asia. In folk practice it is raised at home and swallowed live, and has been promoted for inflammatory conditions, with claims of general wellness.

Its connection to looks is by claim only, through its reputed anti-inflammatory action. Lab and animal studies examine anti-inflammatory and antioxidant extracts, but no trial supports curative effects.
quick.how: In folk practice people keep small colonies of the beetles and swallow them whole, usually as part of a community network sharing breeding stock.
quick.risks: Its defensive secretions contain quinones that are cytotoxic to healthy and cancerous cells in lab studies. Overconsumption is linked to serious complications such as pneumonia, and Wikipedia describes it as contraindicated as a treatment.

lead: Ulomoides dermestoides is a darkling beetle in the family Tenebrionidae, native to Asia and spread worldwide as a pest of stored grain and as a folk remedy. It is known as the Chinese beetle, peanut beetle, cancer beetle or asthma beetle.[1]

In Japanese and Chinese folk medicine it was used for low back pain, cough and asthma. Around 2000, reports emerged of people in Argentina and Brazil raising the beetles at home and eating them live, sharing them through community networks, for conditions from asthma to arthritis.[1] Appearance is not a documented focus, but inflammatory conditions are the closest overlap.
Research includes studies of extracts for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, a rat study of beetle fat in diabetes, and analyses of its defensive secretions; none is a human trial.[2][3][4]

chain: Beetles swallowed live in folk practice
angle.text: Practitioners claim anti-inflammatory benefits; any effect on skin or looks is a claim by extension, not a documented use.

infobox: Chinese beetle, peanut beetle, cancer beetle, asthma beetle[1]

paras: Traditional uses in Japan and China were for back pain, cough and asthma; from about 2000 live beetle consumption was reported in Argentina and Brazil.[1]

Reviews describe the beetle as a source of antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compounds.[2] A 2010 rat study found anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects of the beetle in induced pleurisy.[3] A 2018 rat study examined beetle fat in diabetes.[4] A 2011 cell study found its defensive secretion cytotoxic and genotoxic to lung cells.[5] Wikipedia summarises that medical studies have been mixed, with toxic effects dominating at higher doses.[1]
No studies found. Existing work consists of cell, animal and chemical analyses.[2][3][4][5]
The beetle's quinone-rich defensive secretions are cytotoxic, and overconsumption can cause serious complications such as pneumonia.[1][5]

timeline.event: Reports of live beetle consumption in Argentina and Brazil.[1]
